Immoral describes something — an action, a behavior, a habit, or a person — that goes against the accepted rules of right and wrong conduct. When something is called immoral, it means it is ethically bad, wrong, or wicked, and that it causes harm, unfairness, or offense to people, society, or core human values.

Think of it this way: society, culture, religion, and human conscience together build a kind of invisible fence around behavior — a boundary that separates what is considered right from what is considered wrong. When someone crosses that fence, their behavior is called immoral.

The word has two parts:

  • "Moral" means relating to principles of right and wrong. Something moral is good, decent, and ethically acceptable.
  • "Im-" is a prefix that means not or the opposite of.

So immoral = not moral = against what is right and good.

It is that simple at its core, but the richness of the word goes much deeper, as you will see below.

The adjective "immoral" can describe many different kinds of things:

Actions and behaviors — Things people do can be immoral. Stealing, lying to hurt someone, cheating, abusing a person who trusts you, exploiting the weak — these are classic examples of immoral actions.

People — A person can be called immoral if they consistently act against ethical principles, show no regard for right and wrong, or deliberately cause harm to others without remorse.

Systems and institutions — Even large structures can be called immoral. A law that allows one group of people to be treated as less than human, or a business practice that deliberately deceives and harms customers, can be described as immoral.

Ideas and attitudes — A belief that encourages cruelty, discrimination, or exploitation can also be called immoral.

• "It is immoral to steal from the poor to enrich yourself."
  • "Many people consider animal cruelty deeply immoral."
  • "She refused to participate in what she saw as immoral business practices."
  • "Slavery was not just illegal — it was profoundly immoral."
  • "He was known as an immoral man who lied and cheated without guilt."

In each example, notice that "immoral" is pointing to a failure of character or conduct — a violation of what decent, ethical behavior looks like.

"Immoral" is not a mild word. It carries real weight. When you call something immoral, you are making a strong ethical judgment — you are saying it is not just mistaken, rude, or unfortunate, but genuinely wrong in a deep moral sense. It implies a clear violation of right and wrong, not just a minor social blunder.

Compare:

  • "It was rude of him to interrupt." — a minor social failing.
  • "It was immoral of him to manipulate a grieving widow out of her savings." — a serious ethical wrong.

These three words are often confused, so understanding the differences will sharpen your understanding of "immoral" greatly.

1. Immoral vs. Amoral

This is one of the most important distinctions.

  • Immoral means knowing what is right and wrong, and choosing to do wrong anyway. An immoral person understands the moral rules but breaks them.
  • Amoral means having no sense of right and wrong at all — not caring about morality, or existing outside of moral judgment entirely. A wolf that kills a rabbit is not immoral — it is amoral, because it has no moral awareness.

A con artist who deliberately tricks people is immoral — they know it is wrong and do it anyway. A toddler who accidentally breaks something is not immoral — they are too young to fully understand moral rules.

2. Immoral vs. Illegal

  • Illegal means something is against the law.
  • Immoral means something is against ethical principles of right and wrong.

These two concepts overlap but are not the same thing:

  • Something can be immoral but not illegal — for example, cheating on your partner, lying to a friend, or being deliberately cruel in a way the law cannot touch.
  • Something can be illegal but not immoral — for example, jaywalking, or hiding Jewish families from the Nazis during World War II (which was illegal at the time, but most people would consider it profoundly moral).
  • Something can be both immoral and illegal — murder, theft, and fraud, for instance.

3. Immoral vs. Unethical

These two words are very close in meaning and are often used interchangeably, but there is a subtle difference:

  • Unethical tends to refer to the violation of a specific, often professional or formal set of rules — the ethics of medicine, law, journalism, or business. A doctor who shares a patient's private information is acting unethically because it violates the specific code of the medical profession.
  • Immoral is broader and more personal — it refers to a deeper violation of human values and conscience, not tied to any specific professional code. It speaks to something being fundamentally wrong as a human act.

In practice, something unethical is almost always also immoral, but "immoral" carries a stronger, more personal moral condemnation.
An Important Nuance: Who Decides What Is Immoral?

This is where the word becomes genuinely interesting. The concept of "immoral" depends on a moral framework — a set of beliefs about what right and wrong actually mean. And different people, cultures, religions, and philosophies have different frameworks.

  • A strict religious community might call certain clothing, foods, or relationships immoral.
  • A secular society might call certain discriminatory laws immoral.
  • Philosophers disagree endlessly about what the true foundation of morality is.

However, there is a large area of broad agreement across most human cultures and throughout history — things like murder, cruelty, betrayal, exploitation of the innocent, and dishonesty that causes serious harm are widely regarded as immoral. These shared standards form the strongest and most universally understood uses of the word.

So when you use the word "immoral," it is worth being aware that it is grounded in a moral viewpoint — but it is also a word used to express some of the deepest and most widely shared human judgments about right and wrong.

Synonyms (words with similar meaning):
Wicked, unethical, corrupt, sinful, depraved, dishonest, unprincipled, wrong, indecent, vile.

Antonyms (words with opposite meaning):
Moral, ethical, righteous, virtuous, decent, principled, honorable, good.

Immoral means acting against, or being contrary to, the principles of right and wrong — choosing, promoting, or embodying what is ethically bad, harmful, or wrong, whether in a person, an action, a system, or an attitude.
